St. Croix Cbristi\nsteii, Thursday þÿNovb 19, r 1840. þÿ <?> þÿCJU» Since our last, London papers of the 15th October have been received. We learn by them that Admiral Stopford had sailed to attack the castle of St. Jean þÿd Acre, but the result was not known when the packet þÿsail d. The Fsench Minister, M. Thiers, had addressed a letter to Lord I'almerston demanding to know if England and the other Allied Powers had agreed with the Sultan in deposing Mehemet Ali from the government of Egypt. Lord Palmerston's reply had not been made public at the last dates. It is thought however that the Allies will not sup. port the Sultan in this harsh measure; some accounts state that Russia and England coincide with the Sultan, and Austria and Prussia are opposed to him on this question. The Paris papers say that any interference of the Allies to depose Mehemet Ali from the Government of Egypt will he considered bv France as a justifiable cause of war.

The King of Holland has abdicated his Crown in favour of his eldest son the Prince ot Orange, who had taken over the government. l'he reasons assigned by the old King fpr this step are ivs advanced age, and his desire to live in retirement. The present King must be over Fifty, having served under the Duke of Wellington in the Peninsular Campaigns, and he commanded a Corps of the Allied army at Waterloo, and was wounded at Quatre Eras.

General Espartero, Duke of Vittorin, made a triumphant entry into Madrid, and was received with great acclamations by the people; he was seated in a magnificent Coach drawn by six horses Ail parties look up to him to restore Spain to tranquility and happiness He is at the head of the party þÿcall d Mori, ratios," the other parties are the Emltadat, (radicals), and the high church and state party ot the Ancient Regime. The Queen Regent and her daughter the Queen remained nt Valencia. It is said the former is very desirous of resigning the Regency and retiring from Spain.

New York advices to 28th ultimo are received. Our papers are sanguine of the success of General Harrison, in the present contest for the Presidency, by a large majority. The electors are all chosen by this time, and in two or three weeks we shall know the result Business had much revived at New þÿY ork and Bank Stocks were on the rise. We received last night the Paris papers ot Monday, and the Madrid mail of the 5th. We are still without arrivals from the east and the Paris papers express great disappointment in not receiving some authentic news of the operations ot our squadron. The Castor steamer, with the Levant mail, is now overdue ; but the Government papers assert that she has not arrived, and that no telegraphic intelligence has been received. The capture ol St. Jean þÿd Acre, or the failure of our squadron before it, will, it is expected, be reported by the next arrival ; and it is amusing to observe the two sided opinion which is formed on the subject at Palis. One class ol persons argue, that the fall ol St. Jean d'Acre would ensure the execution of the treaty, and consequently that peace must follow a lact accomplished ; while others contend that a failure would make the English Government more reasonable, and induce it to listen to the councils ol Fi ance. A third party hold, that the capture ol St. Jean þÿd Acre, ora defeat before it, would equally wound the honor of the French nation, as what France complains of is the rigid execution of the treaty. The occupation ol St. Jean þÿd Acre by the English is an event that France can never contemplate with patience, and the attempt to take possession is equally offensive to Gallic pride as the occupation itself. According to the latter opinion war must be the result of our attack on that celebrated fortress ; while, according to the former reasoning, peace is a necessary

consequence. The peace party is certainly the strongest in the Freuch capital at tins monioinent, but our correspondent nevertheless seems to think that the fail ol St. Jean d'Acre would create a renewal of that bad leelino against England which was so decidedly manifested on the taking of Beyrout. The tone and temper of the French press is much more reasonable than it lias lately been, and the pacific language of the English journals ; begins to produce a good effect. þÿ Lvons, Oct. 10. þÿ Yesterday, from nine in the evening till midnight, La Place des Terreaux, and that of the þÿPid ecture, wore the theatre ol disorderly scenes. 1 he þÿ þÿMarseillaise was sung by a crowd composed of several thousand persons. La Place de la Prefecture became immediately a place þÿd armes. Picquets were placed at the head of each street, and large bodies of troops were brought to the immediate neighbourhood. The gendurnerie and the cavalry ol ihe garrison kept the crowd in order in the neighbourhood of the theatre. Thirty persons were arrested, and soon after midnight the tumult censed. The riot was not renewed on the following day, but the mayor of Lyons thought proper to put the law in execution, preventing the assembly of seditious þÿpersons.

The < þÿMarseillaise is nightly played at the theatres of Paris; but it is amusing to remark that, at the minor houses, that air produces very little interest, and it is only at the Grand and the Comic Opera that an impression is created. On Sunday night rows on a small scale took place at both these great theatres, in consequence of the pit demanding that a verse should be sung by the first artist. The demand was complied with at the Opera Cornique, hut M. Dupkez resolutely refused at the Academie Roy ale. The managers of the Paris theatres are in despair at the þÿ "Marseillaise" being licensed by the police, as respectable persons leave the house when the revolutionary hymn begins

October 17 : þÿ Furis, Thursday Evening, 9 þÿo clock. Another attempt has been made to assassinate the King of the French, at 0 þÿo clock this evening. 1P&ST831 From the Boston Courier Nov: 4, 1840. If any ever doubted the intention of the British government to convert their steamships and mail packets to vessels of war, such doubts may be removed by the following from the Standard : þÿ

Steam- vessels as Men-of-War. The numerous steamers which trade between the port of London and various places, could be made available for the purposes of war at a very short notice ; and if only one third of the steam ships belonging to the river Thames were to be armed and provided with ammunition in the event of hostilities, a powerful fleet could be sent against the enemy, while their captains and crews, from their knowledge of the English, Dutch, and French coasts, the channel, &c , would be very serviceable. The admiralty have had their attention drawn to this, and have been recently making inquiries into the condition of the steam vessels, and their capabilities for war, from which it appears that the various companies. without any interruption to their general trade, could provide 50 steam vessels, of from gOO to 1200 tons burthen, which, in three weeks, eould be converted in'o men of war. The General Steam Navigation Company have the largest fleet of steamers of any Hading community in Europe, amounting in all to 40 sail, and among them are many splendid vessels, including the Monarch, equal to any steam ship in her Majesty's service, the Clarence, Giraffe, Ocean, Neptune, Britannia, Countess of Lonsdale, Attwood, Soho, and others, which could easily be converted into war steamers, and make a very formidable display. We believe the General Steam Navigation Company have intimated to the government that they could provide them with a dozen large steam ships on an emergency,

and from this it will be seen that the port of London alone, independent of Liverpool, Hull, Glasgow, and other places, could furnish steam-vessels sufficient for the navy, if Great Britain should be called upon to defend herself against foreign aggressions The papers are almost silent in regard to royal movements. Austria. þÿ The autumnal manoeuvres in the grand camp of the 8th Corps of the German Confederated Army began near Nuremberg on the 2d inst. Great numbers of visitors, have flocked thither to witness them. It is announced that the Government have called into service a portion of the 2d and 3d Battalions of the Landwehr. The 38,000 recruits granted by the Hungarian Diet will make the Army complete. These are not hostile demonstrations, but they show that the Government is ready for any event. There is something very pleasing and manly in the bearing of tfie Uermun Military, Notwithstanding the bravadoes which every day fill the papers of their Gallic neighbours, and the affected certainty with which they at one time talked of conquering the Rhenish provinces in a single march, you hear the probability of a war discussed with thegieatest coolness in Military circles, its chances by no means disregarded, nor the strength of

the enemy undervalued. Tiie French, howpVer, are woefully mistaken if they speculate upon the existence of the slightest relic of that indifference which was the true reason of their success in the revolutionary war. Every European nation which fraternized with these soi disant. liberators received a lesson not easily forgotten, and was taught to its cost that national independence, even when accompanied by some domestic inconveniences, is tbe first possession which the freeman has to defend, and without which to talk of liberty is the bitterest of mockeries.

Yesterday afternoon, shortly after two o'clock, great excitement pervaded the western portion of the metropolis by a rumour that Scott, þÿ the American þÿDiver, who had of late become so notorious by his extraordinary fiats, had met with his death during the performance of his customary evolutions prior to taking his dive from the summit of Waterloo Bridge into the Thames. It appears that in the morning a placard, of which the following is a copy, had been posted throughout the metropolis : þÿ þÿ Challenge to the World for 100 guineas! Monday next Jan 11th. 1841, and during the week. Samuel Scott, the American Diver, wdl run from þÿGodfrey s, White Lion, Drurvlane, to Waterloo Budge, and leap into the water, 40 feet high from the bridge, and return back within the hour every day during the week, between one and two o'clock S. Scott will be in attendance every day at the above house, open to any þÿwager. This notice drew, long before the time appointed, thousands ot persons to Waterloo Bridge, and at five minutes past two o'clock Scott accompanied by several persons, arrived on the bridge He was merely attired in a blue striped shirt and white canvas trowsers, and had on neither shoes nor stockings. On his arrival there could not have been less than from 8000 to 10,000 persons assembled upon the bridge and along the banks of the river. Immediately over the second arch on the Middlesex side and nearest to Somerset

House, was erected a species of scaffolding Composed of two upright poles, and three others crossing them at intervals of about four or five feet, the entire height of which above the balustrades being about 10 feet. Scott appeared as usual, firm and undaunted, and made several jocular remarks to those around him Having ascended the scaffolding, he attached lire rope he carried with him. w hich was about 10 feet long, to the uppermost cross pole, and after placing some tin boxes round the necks of several of his friends w ho were to collect money for him, proceeded to commence his performance, observing, W hy þÿ you all app< ar to be þÿcranky. He first put his head into a noose of the rope, and suspended himself for a minute or twos alter which he placed his feet in a similar position, and swung with his head downwards. He again mounted the top beam of the scaffold and, taking a handkerchief þÿoff his head, placed it on the lop of one of the perpendicular poleslie then seized 'he rope, and placing it round his neck, exclaimed at the top of his voice, « Now þÿI show ll you once more how to dance upon air before I dive þÿ The unfortunate rnan again let himself down to the extremity of the rope with his head in the noose, but had scarcely hung more than three or four minutes when a person named Brown observed that he much feared the man had hung himself in realitv, as animation appeared suspended. þÿ To this one of þÿScott friends s he has not hung half his time þÿyet. In two

or three minutes after, however, shouts were heard in all directions of Cut him þÿdown. Mr. Brown immediately ascended and raised the poor þÿfellow arm. s which on being let go fell heavily back to its original position bv his aide. This gave convincing proof of the sus-

iDAlygas; Tjararxrpiaai BaMjE&HXM pension of animation, and renewed cries were raised from all quarters of þÿ Cut him down.' Some time elapsed before a knife could be procured, and then two persons ascended the ladder, and with the aid of some of the F. division of police, succeeded in cutting the man down Mr. Havers, surgeon of the York road, and another medical gentleman who happened to be upon the spot, immediately stepped forward and opened the jugular vein, and also a vein in the arm, but only a few drops of blood followed ; and to all appearances Scott was lifeless. A cart was then procured, in which fie was conveyed, followed by hundreds of persons, to Charingcross Hospital, when it was ascertained by Dr. Golding, the senior physician, that life was >t quite extinct. Under that gentleman's direction, the unfortunate man was, in the first place, subjected to the galvanic process; secondly, cupped between the shoulders; and then, lastly, placed into a warm bath, in which he had been but a few seconds when it was ascertained that the vital spark had fled. Scott was a remarkably fine young man, about 30 years of age, and, although he called himself an American, was supposed to be a native of Deptford, where he, together with his wife, was residing. She was not, as was her usual custom, with him on the present occasion ; but information of the melancholy affair was immediately dispatched to her on its result becoming known. The cause of the occurrence is not to be attributed, as it was generally rumoured, to

the unfortunate man having indulged in drinking prior to his undertaking his perilous exhibition, but to the meie accidental circum- j ed of the great danger of the slack rope tr.ck, stance of the knot in the noose having slipped from under his chin in such a manner as to produce suffocation. It will be remembered that a similar accident occurred to the celebrated Blackmore, and which almost terminated fatally, a few years since, whilst performing his evolutions at Vauxhall Cardens.

Friday, Feb. þÿ5 J? p. m The United Slates Bank has again exploded This event has taken place sooner than we expected; hut it was looked upon as inevitable within 00 days The demands have been steady upon it for specie, owing, as we intimated some time since, to the total want of confidence on the part of the community in consequence of which, every one pressed to have his demands realized. The absurd stories told by the partisans of the bank, par ticularly the folly of the London letter in the Courier and Enquirer, and the barefaced attempts at imposition by the other papers in the pay of the bank, continued to increase the public alarm, and at half past two o'clock yesterday, the bank, having been drained to the last dollar, closed its doors. In the evening a special meeting was held of the Board of Directors, and the following resolutions were passed : þÿ bank of Tim United States, ) February, 4. 1841. ) At a spceial meeting of the Board of Directors of the Bank of the United States, held at the Banking House, the following preamble and resolutions were unanimously adopted : þÿ Whereas the Bank of the United States, in compliance, with its pledge to the public, has made a fair and bona fide effort to resume and maintain specie payments, having since the 15th of January last, paid out an amount little, if at all, short of six millions of dollars, in coin or specie funds And whereas, the effoit to maintain specie payments by this bank, has been rendered abortive by the in-

tentional accumulation, and extraordinary enforcement of its instant liabilities: þÿ Therefore, Resolved, That the bank is under the necessity, for the present, of suspending specie payments. Resolved, That every exertion will be made by the Directors, to collect the debts, ( one after another, until the four above named and convert into cash, the assets of the bank, j were all that paid in full at 3 o'clock. for the purpose of resuming payments in specie, at the earliest practicable moment. Resolved, That the foregoing preamble and resolutions be published. Extracted from the minutes. A. Lardner, Cashier. M'Le.od. þÿ An extra of tli e Lockpnrt Courier, published on Saturday, gives an official account of the public meeting held in the case of þÿM Leod. It appeals that on the fact being known on Wednesday evening, that þÿM Leod had been admitted to bail, some four or five hundred citizens assembled spontaneously at the Court House, and organized into a meeting by the choice of John Jackson, as Chairman, and Wiixiam O. Brown, Secretary. A Committee was then appointed to wait on Judge Bowen, and Messrs. Buel and Brotherston the reputed bail, to ascer. tain if the report was true. The Chairman meanwhile having stated to the meeting, that if Mr þÿM Leod had entered into bail, he was entitled to a discharge from prison, and that I October. The dates ate any attempt to obstruct his discharge would subject the offender to severe punishment, the following resolution was adopted: Resolved, Vital no obstruction to the discharge of s .id þÿM Leod in case lie has entered n'o Hail, shall he made or countenanced, but that it is the right and duty of this meeting, considering the circumstances of the case, and that the amount of bail is far unequal to the demand of the law, (if bail be allowed at all,) to try to prevail on Messrs. Buel and Brotherston to surrender said þÿVl Leod to the Sheriff, a privilege which bail in all cases possess. The meeting then adjourned to 9 o'clock on the following morning; at which time the

Committee reported. At this meeting Judge Bowen and Captain Buel, were present, and arrangements were made for the legal surrender of þÿM Leod by his bail. A Committee was then appointed to embody the sentiments of the meeting in a series of resolutions, which were reported and adopted after the following fashion : Whereas, the case of arrested and held to bail for a capital offence, has become a matter of serious importance, and to which the attention of our fellow citizens, in every part of the country is directed, we as citizens of the village of Lockport, and county of Niagara, feeling anxious that such steps should be taken in the matter, as shall be consistent with our rights, the supremacy of our laws, and a vindication of our national honor, disavow all intention of prejudging the case of said Alexander þÿM Leod or to do aught that shall have a tendency to prevent said AT Lend from having a fair and impartial trial, acting on the legal maxim, that the accused should be piesumed innocent until proved guilty. Therefore, Resolved, That we are highly gratified that Capt. Wm. Buel has seen fit to place þÿM Leod again in custody, especially as it is but a few days before the sitting of our Court, when the Grand Jury will pass upon his ease, under the direction of the Court. Resolved, That we highly approve the recent answer to Mr Forsy th to the unjust demand of Mr Fox for the discharge of the said þÿM Leod, and the sentiments of Messrs. Fillmore, Cushing and Alford, delivered in

Congress, fully meet our approbation, and are such as the exigency of the ease and the honor ofthe nation called for. Resolved, That all cause of dissatisfaction in relation to the bailing of þÿM Leod has been removed by the course taken by Judge Bowen and Capt. Buel, and that therefore this meeting stand adjourned without day. Such is the face put upon this affair by its Cilicia! chronicles, authenticated by the signa-

Lockpokt, Feb 1. 1841. The undersigned þÿ the counsel of Alexander Mc'Leod, now a prisoner in this country, on a charge of murder, þÿ in view of the very exaggerated and erroneous statements concerning the objects of the attempt to procure his discharge upon bail, þÿ and actuated by ihe belief that those statements tend, though they may not be designed, to prejudice the cause of our client, before the people, from whom a jury, in case he shall be indicted, must be obtained þÿ feel called upon to submit to the public an unvarnished history of the transaction. Mr. þÿMc Leod was committed to the jail of this county about the 18th of November last. But the mittimus being void on its face, we procured the allowance of a habeas corpus with a view to his dischatge. At the hearing before Judge Bowen, the District Attorney conceded the nullity of the process, but suggested, nevertheless, that the judge had jurisdiction to hear proofs anew, and to recommit if ptobable cause should be shown. To this

Mr. þÿMc Leod did not object, but desired such an examination as would satisfy ali of his innocence. and save him from harassing repetition of arrest, þÿ he having several weeks before. been arrested for the same charge, committed to jail, and finally discharged on habeas cm pus la accordance with this desire, it was suggested that he give bail to appear at the next court competent to try him, and, if indicted, have the matter passed upon by a jury of the country. To this. Mr. þÿMc Leod deprive readily assented ; and the judge of his own motion, fixed his bail at five thousand dollars, an amount which the undersigned then believed, and now believe, amply sufficient to secure his presence at the trial. The prisoner then returned into custodv( there to remain until his friends in Canada should give an indemnity to some person residing here, to become his hail. Not being able to effect this, however, as goon as he expected, be determined to be again brought before the judge, and then underwent another examination That officer, however, for reasons doubtless satisfactory to himself, saw fit to remand him, unless he gave the bail required above. He was accordingly remanded Being closely imprisoned, be did not succeed in obtaining bail until the 20th ult., when two gentlemen, residing in or near Chippewa, U. C., gave William Bucl and l\ C. H. Brotherson, of this county, their bond to save them harmless, and the latter entered into the necessary recognizances; and an order was

made hv Judge Bowen, discharging Mr. þÿMc Leod from impiisonmcnt. But the order was not obtained until nearly nightfall ; and owing to a rumour that there were persons about the county prepar ed to commit upon Mr. þÿMc Leod personal

While these proceedings were going on below, a meeting of several hundred men was organized in the Couit Room above. þÿ About 12 o'clock at night, committees were appointed to wait upon the Judge, who had granted the order, and upon the gentlemen who had become þÿMe þÿLena bail, s and lequest their immediate appearance, 4 lie Judge, we understand, deemed it most piudent for him to get out of bis tied, and obey the summons. in and about the jail, the rerna nder of ihe night. In the morning, accordingly, was presented the novel spectacle of an aimed guard, marching with measured tread, in front of ihe Court House door þÿ and this, too, in a lime of peace, and a government ot Law, and with no other assignable motive, than to an individual of rights, which that Law, through its own proper officers, hud conferred. In the meantime, an express had been despatched to Buffalo, to advise a Mr. Wells, that Mc'Leod was about to be discharged ; and to procure a writ whereon lie might be again arrested in an action horn the damages arising from his alleged agency in the destruction of the Caroline. At the re opening of the meeting'in the morning, t lie messenger, having now returned, announced that lie had accomplished the purpose of his mission. þÿ Whereupon, he exhibited lo ihe assembly, a capias, at the suit of Wells, with a þÿJudge s order to hold þÿMc Leod to hail, in the sum of seven thousand dollars. This process, afier having been examined by several individuals, and pronounced to be in due form, was put into the hands of one of the Sheriffs Deputies, and soon afterwards served. After the Captain of the Watch had formally reported the occurrences subsequent to the adjournment, a great variety of motions and propositions were made and discussed. þÿ Among them was one, whether the suit commenced by that capias might riot be settled by the plaintiff and defendant ? An affirmative answer being given, it was followed by a
motion, tfial þÿ thebail surrender Mc'Leod þÿimmediately. But it being suggested and

given I fie assembly to understand, that ote of the bail had given satisfactory evidence ot hie willingness to do so, that motion was withdrawn. Whereupon, another, þÿ thatthe meeting do riot adjourn, until a surrender had been þÿcompleted, was adopted without a dissenting voice. Various legal questions, involving the jurisdiction of the Judge t<> recominil, þÿ of the bail to surrender, þÿ the t fleet of an unexecuted order for a previous dischaige, and the requisite formalities to make a surrender effectual, were mooted, and alter the Judge and District Attorney (who had been brought up again by a fresh committee) as well as other individuals had teen heard, were, satisfactorily to the meeting, disposed of. Feeling the force with which the existing state of things gave these admonitions, he at length concluded to follow the advice of the meeting. At about half past one o'clock in the afternoon, by a sugt.lar coincidence, the same Judge, who had been the cause of this great commotion, by letting Mc'Leod to hai , announced that a surrender in due form of law had been made Whereupon the assembly, formerly, resolved, that

its object was accomplished, and then adjourned. In submitting the foregoing detail of facts, our purpose is not to cast censure upon any one ; for whatever may te our own opinions of these tiansactions, this is not the time, or the place, to express them Our sole object is to protect ihe interests of our client. We are advised, that an , Hurt is already in progress. to persuade the public, that the object of bailing þÿMc Leod was to avoid a trial. þÿ Knowing that no such design existed for a moment, we feel called U|<>n P> repel the charge at once, that the conviction of its tt nth may not settle upon the public, and opeiate to bis prejudice on trial. Foi ourselves, we not only believe Mr. Mc'Leod to hr entirely innocent of the clraige, but it is what we have no doubt upon. And it is painful to us, to witness the dibit now making, to procu. c an universal condemnation of him. bv the public press, and through that, by the whole body of the people, without having heard one particle of the evidence on either þÿside not content with fanning, to his prejudice, the excitement already existing on the subject of the Caroline, a portion of the. press has recently been gleaning, on the other side of the river, for materials (whether true or false, is alike, unimportant), for farther attacks upon this defenceless individual, and that too, upon subjects having no connection whatever, with the matter with which he stands charged ; attacks, the only possible effect of which must be, to render it yet more

difficult than it has already become, to find among those, who are to he his triers, that strict impartiality, which the law guarantees to every one, no matter how slight mav be the ofiencc, for which he may be arraigned. In these circumstances, it seems to us. that is not only our right, hut our duty to nj |,ai þÿ not to the sympathies, þÿ but to the sense of justice of our fcliuw citizens, ana ask them,

until they shall have heard his cause, to sus. pend their judgments, as to the guilt or innocence of this man, þÿ a foreigner, in prison, and beset so recently, by a power which places itself above the law, and arraigns before it those very officers by whom the law has declared its own decrees shall be pronounced. In making this appeal to American citizens, whose pride it is to ad ninister to all, evi n handed justice, we are confident we shall not appeal in vain. A. C. BRADLEY. H. GARDNER.

The principal items of news, consist in the temporary failure at least, of the expedition against China and the discus ftinn of the affair of ttie Caroline iit the British Parliament. The apprehension of þÿMc Leod, has, it will be percpived, excited great indignation in England, and roused a war feeling, which it will require great prudence and foresight in the two governments to allav ; and which until then, cannot fail to have a very injurious effect upon American securities and credit. The Press of course, is loud in its denunciations of this country ; and both parties in Parliament united in the opinion that it was a National affair involving the honour of the British Nation. We content ourselves with laying before onr readers, the answers of the British Ministry to the questions propounded to them » from which it will he perceived that Lord Palmerston not only justifies the capture of the Caioline as a necessary measure of selfdefence, tint distinctly asserts that both our Minister in London, and our Government at Washington, had tteen apprised o| the sentiments of the Biitish Ministry on this subject ! This declaration places the late administration ot VI a criN van Buken þÿ we say late, for thank God it expired at 12 þÿo clocklast night þÿ in no enviable position before the country.

In connexion with tins subject, we have heard it said, that Mr Stevenson, immediately after making the demand upon the British Goveminent in 1839 to disclaim the proceeding, received a note from Lord Palmerston, justifying to the fullest extent the capture of the Caroline! An I that thereupon, Mr Ste vknso.n called upon Lord Palmerston, and asked him to withdraw said note of justification, because it placed Mr. Van Boren in a verv awkward predicament, and might lead to a war I Can this lie true? We only state the rumor as it reached ijs long since ; and even now would look upon it as utterly inere.lihle, did we not imagine that we per ceivn a coutii mation of it in Lord Palmerþÿston s replv to Lord Stanley, wherein he sa vs, þÿ l Hither think that my honorable þÿ friend will Jind in that correspondence, that þÿ instruct inns from the American Government þÿ were given to Mr Stevenson to abstain "from pressing the subject þÿ / / This in onr opinion denotes a familiarity with Mr. Stevenson's instructions, which could only arise from »om e tampering on this subject disgraceful to the character of American Diplomacy and to t he Administration which countenanced it We doubt not tint the administration of Gen. Harrison will deem it necessary to investigate ibis subject. The question which now arises, is, will there be war ( There unfortunately exists a small party in this ciij who are bent upon erving out war, war. without anv regard to the state of the country or our existing rela-

tions with Great Britain. When a war does come, whelliei necessary or not, we shall ho found sustaining it ; but, manifold as are our causes of complaint against England, we will yet believe that the peace of the two noun tries so necessary and advantageous to both, cannot and will not be dtslui lied. True, we

T>ATT!vT. TTT'TXi: have demanded that England should disclaim the affair of the Caroline, and she has peremptorily refused to do so. This it appears, Mr. Van Bit ren and lus administration knew hot have kept concealed, and now turn the whole subject over to t heir successors iri the Govern ment. And what is more disgraceful with a full knowl dge of this fact they have made no preparations to meet an emergency which may arise from their own act. If war should ensue, it will he because the Administration of Martin Van Buren made a demand it shrunk from enforcing, and concealed from the country England's reply to that demand ! Base as was this course, it was still more base þÿ still more treacherous to the great trust reposed in them, not to place the country in a position, to enforce if necessary, that demand.

Fortunately for the Country the Whigs are now in power; and since the late administration have by their acts, confessed their utter inability either to advance or recede in this affair, and it left to the wisdom of their successors to arrange, we will not doubt their ability to do so, without in any way compromitting the National Honor. England says she was justified by the Law of Nations in the destruction of the Caroline; we deny her position ; an<i thus the question at once becomes one which may safely he submitted to the arbitration of a third power, because all nations, arc equally concerned with ourselves, in settling so important a question of National Law We predict therefore, that this queslion will be settled by arbitration, the croakings of alarmists to the contrary notwithstanding ; and vve indulge the hope that the Goveminent of England will perceive the necessity arranging at an early day the other of questions in dispute between us. We will not believe that either Mr. þÿO Connel in tiie British Parliament, or Mr. Pickens on the floor of the House of Representatives, will be able to involve the two countries in war ; and if England will but act justly in regard to the | North eastern Boundary and her interference with our commerce on the coast of Aluca, we shall entertain no apprehensions in tegai d to a war.

We take it for granted, that in the existing state of affairs between the two countries, all the rights and injuries of New York growing out of the Caroline affair are necessarily merged in those of the nation ; and that our Slate Courts have no longer any jurisdiction in the case. The recent debate in Congress so entirely pacific in its nature, will go far towards allaying the war feeling in England, and we may therefore, safely conclude, that in a few weeks the intelligence from England, will be far more pacific.

St. Croix Christiansted, Thursday April 1, 1841. By the Barque Condor, Captain Ward arrived on the 30th ultimo, we have, received New York Gazettes to the 14 til March. By some extracts from these papers it will he seen, that nothing positive was known as to the nature of the despatches pr: President, at the latest date. Rumour was busy with her thousand longues in disseminating all kinds of warlike reports. The new administration, having scarcely had time to organise, has been probably the cause of some delay in the, correspondence between the British Minister and the American Secretary of State on the Mac from Lend affair. The, Steam Ship President sailed New York for England on the 1 \ th nil without carrying any decisive reply to the demands which have been probably made by the British Minister relative to the release of Mac Lead. In fact, Mr; Fox was not presented to President Harrison till the 9th ultimo, with the rest of the Diplomatic Corps at Washington In the mean time a general impression appears to prevail, that as the most respectable testimony have declared that Mc'Leod was not on board the Caroline, when destroyed, that his liberation must follow as a matter of course-
From the New York Morning Courier and Enquirer, March 11, 1841.

Was ii i kotow, March 9, 1841. The city is filled with rumours as to the character of the late despatches from England ; the demands made by Mr. Fox upon this Government, &e. tkc. By some, it is said, that the British Minister requires the immediate release of Mc'Leod, or that passports be granted him within ten days. Such idle tales are lepeated by me only to expose their folly. The plain truth is, as yet no demands or other official communication has taken place between Mr. Fox and the new administration. Mr. Webster was engaged vesterdav in the Supreme Court. This may have been the cause why Mr. Fox has not seen him ; but it is more probable, that the ceremony of presenting the British legation to the new Executive should first take place, which has been done this day.

PRESENTATION OF FOREIGN MINISTERS. The members of the Diplomatic Body, now in Washington, and accredited to the Govermnent of the United States, were received by the President yesterday, at 2 o'clock. þÿ Mr. Fox, the British Minister, on being presented bv the Secretary of Slate, made to the President the following address: Sir: I have the honor to address vou in the name of the Diplomatic Body accredited to the United Stales of America. We hasten, sir, to congratulate you upon vour accession to the high office of President of this Republic, which the confidence of your fellow citizens has conferred upon you. We speak the true sentiments of our respective Governments, and countries in offering this testimony of regard and respect for your person and for your station. We rejoice, sir, to have heard from your own lips, in your Inaugural Address, the declaration of a virtuous desire to promote the relation of national friendship and peace between the United Slates and Foreign Powprs ; and we are happv to recognise, your personal character and quali- in ties, the strongest assurance that the efforts of your Government will be faithfully directed to accomplish so wise and noble a purpose. To this address the President of the United States made the following reply :

Sir : I receive with great pleasure the congratulations you have been pleased to offer in the name of the distinguished Diplomatic Body now present, the Representatives ot the most powerful and polished nations with whom the Republic which has honored me with the office of its Chief Magistrate has the most intimate relations þÿ relations þÿ which 1 trust no sinister event will, for ages interrupt. The sentiments contained in my late address to mv fellow citizens, and to which you have been pleased to advert, are those which will continue to govern my conduct through the whole course of my Administration. þÿ Lately one of the People, the undisputed sovereigns of the country, and coming immediately from amongst them, 1 am enabled, with confidence, to say that in thus acting 1 shall be sustained by their undivided approbation. I beg leave to add, sir, that both from duty and inclination 1 shall omit nothing in my power to contribute to your own personal happiness and that ot the friends of whom, on this occasion, you represent, as long as you continue amongst us. The other Ministers with their Secretaries and the persons attached to their respective Missions, were successively presented to the President. lhe Minister of Russia, we learn, was prevented from being present, by indisposition, which, we are happy to be able to say, is not serious þÿ A at. War and Rumours of War þÿ Our city was thrown into unusual commotion yesterday morning, by the announcement that an Express had arrived from Washington with a message from the Slate Department to Governor Sewaiiij apprising him that the British Minister had made a demand for þÿMc Leod in obedience to instructions from his Government, accompanied with an intimation that if the demand was not complied with, he was instructed to close his mission, or in the Ian guage of diplomacy, demand his Passports ! þÿ Mr. Fii.lmoiie our member of Congress tri m Buffalo, was said to be the Bearer of these all important and warlike despatches. We soon satisfied ourselves however, that no such express had arrived ; that Mr Fillmore was in Philadelphia, having left Washington on Monday morning, and who might and would have reached this city at 12 þÿo clock Aitkins Cecelia on Monday night if he had been entiusted with any such despatches ; and that Governor Sewaiid who is now in this City, had received no communication from the State Department on this or any other subject. VVe therefore placed on our bulletin a contradiction of this ridiculous stock jobbing rumour. But the fact is, there is as little basis for the rumour of war, as there is truth or justice in the absurd and foolish prediction of consequences, should it come. We are advised that up to Monday, the Foreign Minister had not been presented to President Harrison, and of course that no communication has been made by the British Minister to the « Secretary

of State. That Mr. Fox will demand the release of Mr. Mc'Leod, now that the British Ministry has gravely and deliberately assumed the responsibility of destroying the Caroline and declared that the English nation holds itself responsible (or that act, we do not doubt ; and we are equally satisfied that our Government will not war against the agent when the principal avows her responsibility. But it does not follow, that war is to be the consequence of this state of things. War, if it come at all, can only be the result of nego tiation failing; and It will he found that neither England nor the United States, will rush heedlessly into hostilities. We do not pretend to sav that the question is without its difficulties ; but we are well satisfied that it can and will he arranged satisfactorily to both parties, and without in any way compromitting our national honor.

St. Croix Christiansted, Thursday May 6, 1841. London advices to the 1 st ultimo are received by the first April packet The repot ts of the probability of a war with the United States had a good ileal subsided. New York dates of the 15 th March had been received in England. which although they brought intelligence that the Mc'Lcod case was not taken out of Court, yet, as they expressed the opinion that his life could not be jeopardized in any event, it had the tendency of much allaying the public feeling on this point in England. Mr. Lahouchere had brought a bill into parliament reducing the import duty of many articles in their West India Colonies, and admitting American fish, (now prohibited) into them. The duties on Flour, Lumber <$-c were to be reduced one half, but nothing is said of reducing the Sugar duties in England, although meetings have been called in a number of large cities, to petition for the reduction of the duty on Sugar, Coffee, 'limber and for the repeal of the Corn Laws. It is supposed, the Government do not like to recommend a reduction of the Sugar duties, ( although it would be very popular,) for fear of injuring their W. I. Colonies

The Courrier Francois confirms the correctness of ihe report that M. Guizot had declared his willingness to sign a convention for the settlement of the Eastern question. It adds, that France lias already virtually withdrawn from her isolation, and that the only conditions stipulated for by M. Guizot are, as we have already stated, that the Bosphorus and Dardanelles shall be closed against ships of war of all nations and that there shall be such a modification of the hatti seheriff as shall secure to Meliemet Ali the fulfilment, both in spirit and in letter, of the terms which were promised to him on the part of the l'orte by England. The Marseilles papers supply details of the las attempts at insurrection in that city, from which it would seem to have been of a much more seiious character than was at first supposed. The plot appears to have originated with the Propagandists, through the agency of secret societies in the south, which extended to Avignon. Nismes, Carpentras, Montpellter, and Carcassonne, the last-mentioned town being one of the most disaffected in that part of France. A movement was contemplated on the night of the 23d, when the Republicans expected to be supported by the labourers employed on the Marseilles canal. The leading feature of the conspiracy was to set fire to the port, and, taking advantage of the panic which would thus be created, to seize on the bank and other public buildings. The authorities, however, having received an intimation of what was going on, placed

gens d'armes at all the outlets of the roads leading to the Canal, whilst police agents in disguise were employed to watch the place of rendezvous (a guingelte bearing the sign of the Polonais). No sooner had the Republicans assembled within the carbaret, than it was surrounded by from 250 to 300 police and gens d'armes. A premature discharge of fire arms enabled many of the offenders to escape, but 17 were captured in the house,

The arrival of the Levant mail has put us in possession of letters and journals from Alexandria to the 7th instant, Constantinople to the 8th, and Malta to the 17tii inst. The contents of these advices are of more than ordinary interest, and show clearly that if the Eastern question be not as much embroiled as ever, it is at least far from a final settlement. The accounts from Constantinople brought by the Smyrna journals announce tfic arrival of the Reiki Sfievet steamer from Alexandria, with dispatches from Said Muhib Elfendi, the envoy of the 1'orie, in reference to the modifications demanded by Meheniet Ali in the hatti scherifi which re invests him with ihe hereditary government of Egypt In a letter addressed by the I'acha to the Grand Vizier, and communicated by him to the Ambassadors of the Four Rowers, he required þÿ 1. That he should have the right of choosing his successor. 2. That his successor should not be obliged to proceed to Constantinople to receive his investiture from the Rorte. 3 1 hat his superior officers should be appointed by him and his successors, and not by the Sultan. 4. That payment of tri buie should be remitted by the Sultan for a limited period, in order that he might apply the entire of the public revenues to the amelioration of the condition of the inhabitants of Egypt. Mehemet Ali, consequently, objects to the commission of surveillance mentioned in the ninth paragraph of tht hatti þÿscfieritl'. States Immediately on the receipt of these dispat

ches the Ministers of the Rorte held an extraordinary council, at which it was resolved to refer the points in issue to the parties to the treaty of Juiy 15, before any difinitive answer should be returned. The advices from Alexandria represent Mehemet Ali as resuming his military preparations, as it still determined to resist in the event of the original terms of his compact with the Rorte not being agreed to þÿ After dispatching his remonstrance to the Sultan, he left Alexandria to visit his son Ibrahim at Cairo. Rumours of the death of the latter personage had reached Alexandria, but prove to be unfounded The object of Mehemei's visit to tiis son is doubtless to concert measures for their mutual defenae, in the event of matters coming to extremities. The Malta Times, Mediterruneo, and Fortafoglio to Ihe 18th, have readied us. They are unusually barren of news, naval or otherwise- Admiral Stopford was expected to leave Malta in the Rrincess Charlotte about the middle of March, to proceed to Corfu, and thence to England. þÿ -»ooo»i þÿ FRANCE AND THE FOUR POWERS. (From the Morning Fost ) The following communication has just reached us The circumstances under which we have been favoured with it are such as leave on our mind no doubtsof its accuracy: þÿ " PARIS, Sunday Evening. " I write to impart to you not an unlooked for, hut still a very important, piece of news- " Many a Council has sat in judgment upon the great Eastern treaty, with which the ruling powers here have, very naturally,
been coquetting, as in some sort an apology for withholding from it their immediate consent, but, whatever may have been the ob-

stacles and objections, bv Wednesday or Thursday, at latest, the draft of ihe new compact will have been returned to the hands of the Baron de Bourquency, unless, indeed, some schism should yet arise among the ministers, or some difference between them and their royal master. The great difficulty has been the national amour propre stimulated by M. I hiers, and pushed advisedly, and for the sake of leaving no retreat, into demonstrations on a scale of extravagance which the nation will rue for many a year. But M. Thiers's tricks are exposed; the nation is disgusted, and the treaty will he in London within 24 hours after this letter reaches you.'

From the American, Several letters have reached the United describing the horrible ravages of the African or yellow fever on board the United States station vessel Dolphin and Grampus. We have, however, seen hut one letter, or extract of a letter, written by Maxwell Woodhull, acting master of the Dolphin, speaking of the success of the expedition against the native kings and pirates, on the coast of Africa. From this extract it appears the Dolphin and Grampus woiked their way amidst very many obstacles, up the narrow river Nunez, to the town of Wilkedi, the principal place or capital of the King of Seharah, a potentate who some time since conceived he might plunder American vessels and abuse and ill treat their crews with impunity. To punish this worthy was the object of the expedition. Wilkedi is situated about 80 miles up the River Nunez. Here the Dolphin and Grampus took a position in which they could soon have reduced the place to ashes. Satisfaction was demanded, and after some boasting and bragging on the part of his sable majesty, it appears he complied with all the demands made on the part of our government, and the two vessels safely descended the Nunez, and arrived, all well, at Sierra Leone, 'ihe river Nunez is so little known that on the best maps we do not find the name of a single town laid down. The pirates ori the river had, however, made themselves so notorious and offensive, that our government deemed it of importance to put an end to theii depredations, and we
are happy to hear that ('apt. Bell has so successfully and meritoriously eliected the objects of the expedition.

We extract the subjoined matrimonial notification from the Munich þÿJournal: " I am the hereditary possessor of a domain and newly built castle, situate in a beautiful pari of the Bavarian forests. The castle, which has many line spacious apartments, is surrounded with mountains, lovely meadows, and fields, through which rivulets wind, woods for the hunt, and streams for angling ; it stands in a charming valley, wherein the town of Cham, with its many old towers, castles of ancient knights, and ruins of the remotest a ges, inspires the soul with poetical feelings- But however delightful ihe spot may be to those who judge of rural life by the fables of V irgil, Horace, and Delille, I think it very melancholy to behold none but myself in my fine rooms, and to see but mv own person teflerted in my looking glass. 1 have, therefore resolved to marry like other simpletons ; and since it is aliirmcd that marriages are made in heaven, and are but a lottery, to see what heaven may have in store for me, and what fair creature the wheel of fortune may allot .1 me, þÿ with this view I submit my wishes to

The one I wish to marry must lie between 10 and 20 years of age ; she must have fine hair, fine teeth, and beautiful hitle feet Nhe must be horn of honest and good parents, and her fame must he spotless. She must dress elegantly, but plainly, in either silk or vclvel, but no other matenals. Siie must not wear ear-rings, chains, rings, or any silly ornaments ol that description ; neither must sliu wear slippers, caps, ribbands, false hair, &o., nor have her dresses made after existing fashions, nothing being so foolish as to follow other human beings, as cows follow one another. CStie must have her clothes made, and wear them according to her own taste and fancy, heedless of what the herd of fashion women may say about it. She must know or learn how to ride and drive. Sfte must never knit, that being a mere manual occupation to conceal stupidity. She shall be allowed music only if she be perfect in that art, it being tiresome to listen to the bad performers who annoy visiters in so many houses. She shall be mistress of the house in all domestic matters, and 1, myself, shall be happy to yield to her reasonable whims, being a great enemy to slavish obedience and submission, whence, thanks to the church, all quarrels and discontent derive their origin ; ' O but she must accompany me hi all my journeys and excursions, because it is, in my opinion, a shame that a man should go about day and nignt, living in splendour at hotels,

whilst bis wife is left at.home alone, a prey lo ennui She must not, as is the case with most married couples, forget what becomes female dignity, and condescend to be the first to coax her husband, as many a highminded lady is compelled to do in order to humour her uncouth lord. On the day of her marriage she shall receive 40,000 florins in Russian and Prussian state bonds, the interest upon which she will, however, he obliged to spend as may suit her pleasure, no vice being more abominable than avarice. She shall dispose of it as may suit her, as well as lire interest on her jointure; but those interests shall not be capitalized on the principle ol the avaricious, nothing in this world being more stupid than to save for other folks. My principle and wisdom consist in the enjoyment of the pleasures of fife in continual good humour. " I must now say something about myself I am 70 years old. according to the almanac, but only 25, judging by my health & strength- I am always cheerful 1 seek for pleusure wherever the strictest honour admits of it. If. therefore, there exist any where a handsome young girl, willing to bustle about on horseback, in travelling, or at home with an old

man, still hale, hearty, and active, she may write to me, and I will go and meet her, to see her and let her see me, at any place within a hundred leagues of Munich, but not further, engaging on inv word of honour that her name never shall be uttered.
